translation:
Jnaniji Maharaj says that toward that Supreme Being who stands beyond the shade cast either by the burning heat of the threefold affliction or by the shadow of maya's delusion, one should hold the aspiration to offer loving devotion. Such a Paramatma is not scorching with the fierce heat of cruelty, nor is he cool with the coldness of delusion and attachment (moha-maya); the mind has become fixed on offering devotion to such a God.

_Gyaani vapu na vaan varan hau, ren divas nahi hoy |
Aisa agam apaarahu, chinhe virla hoy ||23||_
(For the wise one, there is no bodily form, no hue, no color; for him there is no night and no day. Such a one — unfathomable, boundless — only a rare soul comes to recognize.)

Jnaniji Maharaj says that he who has no bodily shape, no color, no form of any kind, and for whom there is no such distinction as night and day — the deep, boundless essence of such a Paramatma, hardly anyone is able to grasp.

The Shiva Purana, Koti Rudra Samhita, chapter 41, shlok 13, says:

_Na rakto naiva peetashcha na shveto neel eva cha |
Na hrasvo na deerghashcha na sthoolah sookshma eva cha ||_
(He is neither red nor yellow, neither white nor blue; he is neither short nor tall, neither gross nor subtle.)

Not red, not yellow, not small, not big, not gross, not subtle is he. In elaborating on Jivanji's sakhi about God's form and hue, it is said in the Samagam that in Kaliyug the glory of the divine Name prevails, but people do not come to know his form — that is, those devoted to outward ritual (karmakand) fail to grasp the essence of devotion. To illustrate this, Adhyaruji's own words are quoted in the Samagam:

_Kartam darshan aap vakhaane, kaljug Vishnu swaroop na jaane |
Khaan chahu bhav paame Hari Hari - khaan chahu bhav paame ||30||_
(The schools of thought built on ritual observance praise only themselves; in Kaliyug they do not come to know the true form of Vishnu — Hari, Hari — and so they fall, again and again, into the four wombs of birth.)

_Chaturvarna no Raas_ (The Song of the Four Varnas)

The philosophical schools that rest on ritual observance, or on knowledge of the self and metaphysics, engage merely in self-praise (arthavad), extolling their own doctrines, but in Kaliyug they do not understand the secret of the love-natured devotion (prem-lakshana bhakti) owed to Vishnu, and so they fall prey to the fear of birth and death in the four wombs.

Charvak, Madhyamik, Yogachar, Sautrantik, Vaisheshik, and Aahat — these six schools are called nastik (atheistic), because they do not accept the authority of the Vedas ( ). Alongside them, Sankhya and Mimansa, though described as non-theistic (anishwarvadi), are counted among the astik (theistic) schools.

The astik darshans are six: Nyaya, Vaisheshik, Sankhya, Yoga, Mimansa, and Vedant. Because they accept the Vedas, they are called astik darshans.

All twelve of these darshans together mark out a sequence in the unfolding of thought. In short, whatever religions, doctrines, or sects have arisen out of India and spread through the world all rest, at their root, on these very twelve darshans. Because of differences in interpretation and exposition, and the diversity that has crept into conduct and practice, the number of sects has grown very large; yet, without an understanding of the ultimate truth that is genuine devotion, ritualism, the path of knowledge, the path of yoga, the path of spirituality, and the rest each cling to their own doctrine and opinion, and so the soul cannot attain liberation.

With reference to such self-serving argument (arthavad), the Gita says:

_Yaamimaam pushpitaam vaacham pravadantyapipashchitaah |
Vedavaadarataah Paartha naanyadastiti vaadinah ||42||_
(Those unwise ones, absorbed in Vedic doctrine, who declare that there is nothing beyond it — and who, craving heaven, hold heaven itself to be the supreme goal — speak such flowery, delightful-sounding words.)

Shankaracharya wrote a commentary on this verse to the following effect: they speak words that seem as beautiful and delightful as flowering trees. Who is it that goes on talking like this? The unwise — that is, people of little understanding, indiscriminate people who remain engrossed in the words of the Vedas that expound self-praise and the means to fruit-bearing ends — saying: "O Arjuna! Such people, holding this very view, maintain that there is no means superior to the actions (that yield results such as the attainment of heaven and the like)."

Just as Adhyaruji does, Jivanji Maharaj too, in describing the workings of Kaal (Time), shows who it is that lives in fear of the four wombs of birth:

_Apni apni jaanme, sab koi bhaye lau leen |
Aapo na chhoote Jivana, jyu paani ko meen ||45||_
(Meaning: each one, according to his own understanding, has become wholly absorbed [in his own doctrine]; and just as a fish cannot leave the water it lives in, so, O Jivan, one's own ego does not let go.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that those who follow their various sects and beliefs have, each according to his own understanding, become utterly absorbed in it, and so their pride and ego cannot free itself from it, just as a fish living in water cannot part from the water.

_Apni apni jaanme, sab ho baithe meer |
Ram naam bin Jivana, jam dware bhai bheer ||46||_
(Meaning: each one, in his own understanding, has made himself a leader; but without devotion to the name of Ram, O Jivan, a great crowd of them has gathered even at the door of Yama.)

Jivanji Maharaj says that every follower of a sect becomes, in his own understanding, a leader or chieftain; but without devotion to the name of Ram, a great crowd of all such people has gathered even at the gate of Yama's hell.

In Sanskrit too there is a verse that criticizes such arrogant people.

_Vaagucchaarotsavam maatram tatkriyaam kartum akshamaah |
Kalau vedaantino bhaanti Phaalgune baalakaa iva ||19||_
(Those who delight only in the festival of eloquent speech, yet are incapable of putting it into practice — such Vedantins appear in Kaliyug like children intoxicated during the Phalgun [Holi] revelry.)

People who revel only in the delight of fine-sounding speech, for whom it is impossible actually to conduct themselves and act accordingly — such people, in Kaliyug, appear like madmen who have grown wild and intoxicated with the frenzy of the Phalgun festival.

Kabirji has said:

_Kabir Shri Krishna jaanya nahi, boho jaane kya hoy |
So Krishnathe sab kachhu hot hai, boho mile kachhu na hoy ||_
(Kabir says: if a man has not come to know devotion to Shri Krishna, then no matter how much else he knows, what benefit is it? Through this Krishna alone can anything at all in this world be accomplished; but however many weaklings gather together, nothing whatsoever can be achieved by them.)

Das Kabirji says that if a person has not learned how to devote himself to Shri Krishna, then even a very thorough knowledge of the Vedas, the scriptures, and the Puranas is of what use? Through devotion to this Krishna alone can whatever one wishes to accomplish in this world be accomplished by God; but however many weak people gather together, they can achieve nothing by it.

_Kabir ek palakme sab kiya, aisa samarath soy |
Aadhya paachha je kare, jo balhina hoy ||_
(Kabir says: in a single instant that all-capable One created everything; but those without strength, working now forward, now backward, produce only confusion.)

Das Kabirji says that God created all of this in the span of a single moment — such is his power; but those who are without strength wander about in confusion, as though piecing together something false and mistaken.

In elaborating this line of Adhyaruji's, the Samagam states that without devotion to Vishnu, all the schools built on ritual and the like fall into corruption. At the start of a yug these darshan shastras arise without it, and by the end of the yug these darshan shastras come to a close and cease.

Hariram Vyas has described the flaws of Kaliyug in a pad set to the raag Sarang. Bhagat Babarbhai Chhotabhai of Shikhodhra has set it down at greater length as follows. The eighteenth pad in the Sarang raag is printed on page 597 of the Panchratnamala, but in Hariram Vyas's own collection, on page 265, it appears as pad number 293 with some variant readings (paathaafer); I therefore present it here in that form.

[Babar Chhota Diary, 1974, p. 209]

Sarang [raag]

_Ab saachehu kalijug aayau |
Poot na kahyo pitaako maanat, karat aapanau bhaayo ||1||_
(Now, truly, has the age of Kali arrived. The son no longer heeds his father's word; he does only as he himself pleases.)

_Beti bechat sanh na maanat, din din mol badhaayau |
Yaahi te barsha mandi hoti hai, punya te paap savaayau ||2||_
(They sell their daughters without a trace of shame, and raise the price day by day; on account of this the rains grow scanty, and sin comes to outweigh merit.)

_Mathura khudatas karat Vrundavan, munijan soch upaayau |
Itano dukh sahibe ke kaaje, kaaheko Vyaas jivayo ||293||3||_
(They dig up Mathura and lay waste to Vrindavan; the sages, in their distress, pondered — for the sake of bearing so much suffering, why was Vyas kept alive at all?)

_Karat Vrudaavan bechat madhukari, Jumna teer sukaayo |
Naari pativrata dharm na paale, sabjug paatak chhaayo ||3||_
(They destroy Vrindavan and sell the alms gathered there; the banks of the Jamuna run dry; women no longer keep the vow of chastity, and sin has spread over the whole age.)

_Sanyaasi dhan sanchan laage, Hari sumaran bisraayo |
Raja kutil praja dukh paave, Braahman Ved bikaayo ||4||_
(Renunciants have taken up the hoarding of wealth and have forgotten remembrance of Hari; kings turn crooked, and their subjects suffer; Brahmins sell the very Vedas.)

_Kulko dharm koi nahi maane, man paakhand lagaayo |
Harijan chhodi krutadhni pooje, bahu vidh dhong machaayo ||5||_
(No one honors the customs of family and lineage any longer; the mind inclines toward hypocrisy; people abandon God's own devotees and worship the ungrateful instead, and pretense of every kind is set loose.)

_Bhakti gyan ko marma na jaane, baane bhekh lajaayo |
Satya vachan praani sab chhode, anarath udar bharaayo ||6||_
(No one knows the true essence of devotion and knowledge; even the ascetic's own garb has been disgraced by those who wear it; all beings have abandoned truthful speech, and fill their bellies through wrongdoing.)

_Patij chhodi dhan kaaran maare, mitra bandhu patijaayo |
Kshatri Ved padhe taji raksha, munikko bhekh banaayo ||7||_
(Abandoning trust, they kill for the sake of wealth even those — friend and kin — in whom trust was placed; Kshatriyas give up the duty of protection and take up the study of the Vedas instead, assuming the guise of sages.)

_Dharat Shudra upveet Viprahon, aasan darbh bichhaayo |
Saadhu Shudra hoy teerathme, aashram baandaa rahaayo ||8||_
(Shudras wear the sacred thread that belongs to Brahmins, and spread the sacred kusha-grass seat; at places of pilgrimage it is Shudras who pass themselves off as sadhus, building ashrams and settling there.)

_Vaaku duniya Harisam pooje, padjal jutho khaayo |
Durlabh manushya deh paayke, bhakti raah bhoolaayo ||9||_
(The world worships such people as if they were God himself, drinking the water that has washed their feet as though it were holy; having obtained the rare gift of a human body, they have lost the path of devotion.)

_Graam devta teerath ke deva, munijan sahas athaasi |
Ant sangat le bhakti Hariko, santat Ram upaasi ||10||_
(The village deities, the gods of the pilgrimage places, and the eighty-eight thousand sages — in the end, keeping the company of the good, take up devotion to Hari and worship Ram continually.)

_Te sab aisa kaljug dekhi, manme paap udaasi |
Prabhuko sharan graho jan tyaagi, chal gaye pad avinaashi ||11||_
(All of them, seeing such a Kaliyug, grew weary at heart of sin; taking refuge in the Lord and renouncing the world, they departed for his imperishable abode.)

_Gangagiri Govardhan girija, Govind dharni tyaagi |
Rahe jivanrak nivaasi, paapi neech abhaagi ||12||_
(Ganga, Mount Govardhan, Girija [Parvati], and Govind [Krishna] have all forsaken this earth; only the sinful, the base, and the ill-fated remain here as its inhabitants.)

_Dharni bhaar sahan dukh paave, puni puni kampan laagi |
Bahu vidh kasht sahat sab praani, chete nahi nirbhaagi ||13||_
(The earth, bearing this weight, suffers and trembles again and again; all beings endure manifold hardship, yet these luckless ones do not awaken to it.)

_Ghor karaal kaliyugme, gun bad ek hoi |
Tamnamse jo Hari anurage, janm maran mit jaai ||14||_
(In this dreadful, terrible Kaliyug there is one great virtue: whoever, through the divine Name, comes to love Hari — for him the wheel of birth and death is brought to an end.)

_Adham uddhaaran gunkaataaran, het kyon birsaayo |
Yahi apraadh dosh dekhve ke kaaran, Vyaasku kaahe jivaayo ||15||_
(O redeemer of the lowest, deliverer of even the fallen woman [Ganika] — why has love for you been forgotten? Only to witness this very fault, this very failing, was Vyas kept alive.)

Now, truly, Kaliyug has arrived. The son no longer heeds his father's command, and does only as he pleases. He sells his own daughter — feels no shame at all in trading away a girl-child — and raises her price day by day. On account of such sin, even the rain falls short; sinful and wicked deeds have come to outweigh virtue and good works upon the earth. People trample and crush Mathura with contempt, and abandon Vrindavan entirely. The sages and holy men, to escape such a state, came to think: rather than bear this whole calamity of wrongdoing, why did God let devotees like Vyas go on living? (Variant reading: by cutting down the tulsi groves — that is, by transgressing the path of righteous conduct — they beg from door to door and sell it away; or, the wealth that came to them by God's grace they squander on delusion and sensual pleasure, and so the water of the Jamuna dries up, meaning the very flow of loving devotion diminishes.) Women no longer keep the vow of chastity, and sinful conduct has spread through the whole world. Renunciants have taken to amassing wealth, and have forgotten — abandoned — the remembrance of God. Kings are deceitful and scheming, and so their subjects suffer. Brahmins sell the Vedas — that is, they trade in sacred knowledge. No one cares any longer for the dharma of decency, and minds are given over to scheming and deceit. People abandon devotees and holy men and instead serve cheats and swindlers. In this way they have set going pretense of many kinds. They do not understand the mystery of the path of devotion to God, and, taking up a false ascetic's garb, have brought disgrace upon that very garb. All beings have abandoned true honesty and have taken to filling their bellies through wrongdoing; abandoning trust, they loot and kill for wealth, while placing their reliance on friends and kin. Kshatriyas abandon the duty of protection and take up the recitation of the Vedas instead, thereby staining the very identity of sages. Shudras wear the sacred thread that belongs to Brahmins, and sit upon seats of kusha-grass. At places of pilgrimage it is Shudras alone who pass as sadhus and holy men; they build ashrams and settle in as if encamped there. Worldly people regard them as pure as God himself and worship them, and even drink the water that has washed their unclean feet as sacred nectar. Even after obtaining the rare and precious human body, such a person has forgotten the path of devotion to God. The village deities, and the gods of the holy places, and the eighty-eight thousand sages — all of these, having kept holy company, forever devote themselves to God, to devotion to Ram. All of them, seeing the traits of Kaliyug, or seeing the very marks of this age, turned their faces away from the faults of Kaliyug. All of these took refuge in God, renounced the world, and departed for the Lord's eternal abode. The Ganga, Mount Govardhan, [Shiva and] Parvati, and Lord Krishna have all forsaken this earth, and

here remain only the base, sinful, worthless people who live on. The earth must bear the weight of such sinners, and so it trembles again and again — earthquakes occur. All living beings, too, endure many kinds of suffering, yet these unfortunate people understand nothing of it. In this terrible, fearsome age of Kaliyug, there is one great virtue, the best of all: that if one practices devotion to God with true love, the wheel of birth and death comes to an end. That God who is the redeemer of sinners — who delivered even the fallen woman [Ganika] — how could love for devotion to such a God have been forgotten? It was only to witness such failings that you, O God, kept a devotee like Vyas alive.

In speaking of the yugas, the text lends its support by citing the line of supplication from Adhyaruji:

_Jug jug darshan joojva | Swami | vanse jug ant |
Vedan vanse vansta | bahu jug kalpaant ||paaye||_
(In every yug the darshans differ, O Lord; at the end of each yug they perish. The Vedas too decay and pass away, over many yugs and kalpas.)

In every yug, according to that yug, the scriptures, the codes of conduct (smritis), and their teachings of truth are set forth. Whatever conduct is authoritative for a given yug comes to an end when that yug ends, and, once it has changed, the conduct authoritative for the new yug that has begun takes its place. But the supreme truth — the reality of God, the divine Name — does not change even though many yugs and kalpas come to their end.

Manu says:

_Anye krutyuge dharmaas trotaayaam dvaapare'pare |
Anye kaliyuge nrunaam, yug hyaasaanuroopatah ||1||_
(Meaning: as the yug wears on, the dharmas that hold in Satyug do not hold in Tretayug, and those that hold in Tretayug do not hold in Dwaparyug, and those that hold in Dwaparyug do not hold in Kaliyug.)

_Deshaakaalanimittaanaam bhaivedharmo vibhidyate |
Anyo dharmah samarthrasya vishamasthasya chaaparah ||1||
Na hvaivaikaantiko dharmah dharmo heyaabasthikah smritah |
Tasmaadanyah prabhavati so'param baadhate punah ||2||_
(Meaning: dharma differs according to place, time, and circumstance. When conditions are favorable there is one dharma, and in adversity there is a different one; dharma is governed by one's condition. There can be no single dharma that benefits everyone at all times. When a given dharma is found to bring harm rather than benefit, another dharma must be adopted; if that too proves harmful, a third rule is taken up. For this reason, it is nowhere to be seen that one and the same practice has continued on unchanged.)

In support of the line "Vedan vanse vansta, bahu jug kalpaant" — the Veda, that is, the true essence of God (Bhagavat-tattva), does not change even at the end of yugs and kalpas; it is that eternal truth. This is stated in shlok 49:

_Lokaanaam bhaagyaheenaanaam kaliyuge pravartite |
Sansiddhir Vaasudevasya naamnaiva Girije dhruvaa ||49||_
(For people bereft of good fortune, when Kaliyug sets in, O Parvati, liberation comes surely through the name of Vasudev alone.)

For fortune-bereft people, when Kaliyug began, Shiva said: "O Parvati! Through the name of Vasudev alone, liberation is certainly attained." The commentary explains: this is the dharma that manifests in Kaliyug — Mahadev spoke thus to Parvati: "O beloved! In this world of the unfortunate, Kaliyug shall spread far; through the name of Vasudev alone the highest state will be reached. For one who has no faith in the dharma of Vasudev, the divine Name itself will awaken that faith in him."

The Vaishnavs who will establish such devotion firmly will arise in India — this is mentioned in shlok 50:

_Aaryaavartona bhavishyanti vaishnavaashcha punah punah |
Sarvakaamapradaa bhaktyaa shrotriyaah shuddhachetasah ||50||_
(In Aryavart, Vaishnavs will arise again and again — men learned in scripture, pure of mind, who through devotion grant the fulfillment of every wish.)

In Aryavart, Vaishnavs will arise again and again, who will be shrotriya (learned in the Vedas), pure of heart, and who, through devotion, fulfill every desire.

Aryavart means the land of Bharat — the region lying between the Vindhya range and the Himalayas, and between the eastern sea and the western sea; that is Aryavart. The mention of Aryavart occurs in the Bhagavat, Skandha 9, chapter 6, shlok 5:

_Teshaam purastaad bhavannaaryaavarte nrupaa nrupa |
Panchavimshatih pashchaascha trayo madhye pare'nyaatah ||5||_
(O Parikshit! Of the hundred sons of Ikshvaku, twenty-five ruled in the eastern part of Aryavart, twenty-five ruled in the western part of Aryavart, while the rest ruled in the middle of the great Aryavart and elsewhere, to the south and the north.)

In the commentary on shlok 50 it is written: Maharudra said that in this land called Aryavart, one, two, or three Vaishnavs will manifest in Kaliyug. To gather pure teaching in this world, to conduct oneself in pure and righteous practice, and to increase pure-hearted worship and kirtan so as to become free of desire, recognize the Supreme Truth, and accomplish the very purpose of the divine descent — these are the three essentials. Hence the acharyas who appeared were, in order: first Vishnuswami, then Nimbarka, Madhvacharya, and Ramanuja; before them, in this creation, there had prevailed the path of knowledge established by Sanakadik and the others. In this Kaliyug, this line of Vaishnav acharyas will break apart the fourfold path of liberation that had prevailed through the three earlier yugas, and, causing loving devotion to sprout, will deliver the world.

Parvatiji asked Shiva to expand upon the dharma of Kaliyug and to explain in detail why dharma breaks apart at the end of a yug. Thereupon Shivji said: once, when the Lord lay resting, his right arm gave a twitch. At that, Lakshmiji said, "O Maharaj! I wish to see the play of your Krishna-form, show me that leela of divine delight — in the span of a single instant, that is, in the blink of an eye, you bring forth the creation of countless universes, as you once showed Narad your inconceivable play; so from the twitching of your arm it seems to me you are about to descend in your own true form to bring the creation to fulfillment. For that reason, be pleased to let me too behold your leelas of raas and your divine deeds." At this Bhagwan said, "You will suffer greatly on account of it." Lakshmiji replied, "I have a great longing, so please fulfill my heart's desire — and since Brahma's sons, the Sanakadik, have renounced maya, seeing this leela would bring karmic consequence upon them; so arrange it that they may come here only with permission, and leave only with permission." But Bhagwan said nothing in reply. Then Lakshmiji told the doorkeeper to inform her whenever the Sanakadik should come. At that time, Brahma's sons, the Sanakadik, came to Vaikunth to have darshan of Shri Hari; Jay and Vijay, seeking Govindji's permission, said "wait" and, holding their staffs crosswise, stopped them from entering. At this the Sanakadik, whose darshan of Hari's abode had thus been obstructed — as ones whose vision they judged unworthy — declared, "You people are not fit to remain here," and pronounced upon them the curse that they be born in demonic wealth, in the wombs of demons. Because of this, the two doorkeepers, stripped of their radiance, bowed to the Sanakadik and began pleading forgiveness for their offense. Seeing this from a distance, Shri Hari came there, comforted them all, and said that this had happened by his own will; he told the doorkeepers, with grace, that after three incarnations they would return once more here to Vaikunth, and asked them to remember and worship his own name as atonement for their offense — and in this way he settled the minds of the Sanakadik and granted them his darshan.

Shri Jivanji Maharaj said that even in Vaikunth, from greed, delusion, and anger, the thought of pronouncing a curse arose in the minds of the Sanakadik — the cause of this anger being that the Sanakadik had come to have darshan of Shri Vishnu Paramatma, who dwelt there in the form of the image of Hansa-Narayan, their own guru,

and, finding themselves obstructed there, they began to think within their own minds, "Why should we be stopped here at all?" In thinking this way, they forgot the very quality of discernment — of separating milk from water — that their guru had given them; this is the fruit of failing to accept the guru's command and word. On this there is a sakhi:

_Kabir machh bekantaa me sunya, dheemar ke darbaar |
Aankhadiyaa ratanleeaa, kyu padiyaa jaal |
Guru partaape kin kubji, jeet liya jam kaal ||_
(Kabir says: I have heard that even in Vaikunth, at the court of the fisherman, the fish [souls] with eyes like jewels — why did they fall into the net? Yet by the guru's grace, Kubja conquered even Yama, the lord of Time.)

Lakshmiji's mind was set on seeing Bhagwan's leela of divine delight; it is Lakshmi herself who spreads the net of maya through the world. But Brahma's sons, the Sanakadik, show a concern that they not become entangled in this leela; yet even the Sanakadik, who go to the door of Lakshmi-Narayan, forget, through the influence of maya, the teaching that Narayan, in the form of the swan (Hansa), had given them, of discerning milk from water. With reference to this, the Samagam gives this sakhi of Kabirji; this sakhi is given under three headings — Kaal (Time), Chetavani (Warning), and "action without mere words" (karani bin kathani).

Having heard the teaching about maya in the glory of devotion, all the souls, like fish, in their eagerness to practice devotion go to be sold at the court of the great Brahminical order — that is, they fall into the net of Vedas, scriptures, Puranas, mantras, and yantras. So the true guru says: O soul! Your discernment — your eyes — were like jewels, yet how did you come to be caught and bound in that net?

The fish of this ocean of worldly existence, filled with the water of wealth and the like, is the human being devoid of thought for devotion; caught in the net of karma, trapped in the snare of maya, and fallen under the sway of greed, craving, and the rest, he forsakes the very nature of Parbrahm and, attached to the things of the senses, goes to be sold at the court of Yama and his like, falling into the eighty-four lakh species of birth.

The fish has eyes as brilliant as jewels, but the fisherman baits it with a hook wrapped in food laced with iron, and, drawing it into greed, catches it. There is a shlok on this:

_Loham vilokya baahisham vasbhakshyaliptam |
Lubdho hi kashmalamalam shakulo'tilolah ||
Draantam grasaat sacha nishkamanaa duraamaarti |
Prayaati maranam cha kadagraviddhah ||_
(Seeing the iron hook wrapped in tasty bait, the greedy fish, its restless mind bent only on swallowing the food, gulps it down at once, and, pierced through by the barb, suffers greatly and meets its death.)

Adhyaruji says:

_Pahelaa laagyu madhuru mukh, pachhi padyo machh mote dukh |_
(To the fish it tasted sweet in the mouth at first; but afterward, caught by the hook, it suffered greatly.)

To the fish it first tasted delicious in the mouth, but then, once the hook caught it, the fisherman caused it great suffering and killed it.

_Kabir paani bhitar ghar kiya, sejya kiya pataar |
Paasaa chhaadya Ramka, to hum baandhe jaar ||_
(Kabir says: I made my home within the water itself, and made my bed in the very depths — yet the moment I let go of Ram's side, I found myself bound in the net.)

Though one has entered the nectar-like waters of the guru's own mouth, and has taken refuge with the guru, if one then abandons exclusive, one-pointed devotion, then, like fish caught in the fisherman's net, we fall into the trap of ritual worship and its idol-service, and end up bound within the eighty-four lakh species of birth.

Siddhi is attained through five mudras; their durations are as follows:

Chachari — keeping the gaze fixed straight ahead — twelve years
Bhuchari — keeping the gaze fixed on the navel — twelve years
Khechari — turning the gaze upward toward the sky — twelve years
Agochari — closing the eyes and looking within — twelve years
Unmuni — fixing the gaze steadily at the trikuti, the point between the eyebrows above the nose — twelve years

That is to say, through even a single one of these practices, siddhi (spiritual power) is attained, but it does not grant liberation — this too is a path by which one can fall. Thus the Sanakadik, having accomplished the khechari discipline, reached Vaikunth, but the doorkeepers caused them to fall back into the cycle of birth and death.

The jewel-like eyes are the intellect; the mind is the net. The Vedas and Puranas speak of devotion in the manner of "action without mere words," yet people practice ritual observance and idol-worship instead, and so the soul is sold in the marketplace of the eighty-four lakh species. Such was the fate that befell the Sanakadik. They had become renunciants of maya, and had become eternally five-year-old children — their hair was white, their water-pot was white, their courtyard was white — and though desire had no hold on them, still anger and the power of Time arose within them.

Adhyaruji's line describing this episode is given:

_Hari Hari dwar Vaikunthne su rahoe, jotaa navalhoe, munijan maahe praves |_
(At the door of Vaikunth, Hari, Hari, they stood; watching there was a wondrous sight — the sages seeking to enter.)

At the gate of Vaikunth the Sanakadik had come and were waiting there; even though they knew the teaching of discerning milk from water, anger still found its way into their minds — this they failed to understand, and lost their own good sense.

In connection with this episode, Jnaniji's sakhi is given in the Samagam:

_Padel pohochtaa maariyaa, loot liyaa sab maal |
Gyaani nachhane nirkhiyaa, aisaa karadaa kaal |
Pol pohotaa kushalsu, raakhi liyaa sab maal |
Guru prasaade kubji, jeet liyaa jam kaal ||_
(As soon as they reached the doorkeepers, they were struck down, and all their wealth was plundered — such, before one's own eyes, is the harshness of Time. But he who reaches the entrance safely keeps all his wealth intact; by the guru's grace, Kubja conquered even Yama, the lord of Time.)

Jnaniji says that the moment the Sanakadik reached the doorkeepers, the harsh power of Time stripped away all the wealth they had gained — their tapobal, the power of austerity, and the good understanding given by the guru — and destroyed it; this is what can plainly be seen from this very episode. But if one reaches Yama's own messengers securely, with the understanding born of devotion, one will keep intact the whole wealth of one's own welfare, and one will conquer even Time — so Kubja says.

The kundali, the expanded rendering, of this sakhi of Jnaniji's has been written by Trikamdas Gordhandas in his diary of Vikram Samvat 2032, page 179, as follows:

_Pol pahonchtaa paadiyaa, chhin liyaa sahu maal |
Gyaani nayane nirkhiyaa, aisaa karadaa kaal |
Aisaa karadaa kaal, Bhaagvad kahe popaaree |
Bhal bhalaa atvai jaay, maayaa chhe bahu thagaaree |
Trikam gurugam jhaal, nugaraa jagmaa haariyaa ||_
(As soon as they reached the gate they were struck down, and all their wealth was seized — such, before one's own eyes, is the harshness of Time. So harsh is Time, the Bhagavat proclaims openly — even the greatest and best go astray in its grip, so deceitful is maya. Trikam says: hold fast to the guru's teaching — those without a guru are defeated in this world.)

Jnaniji says that as soon as they reached the doorkeepers, the harsh power of Time snatched away all the wealth of their tapobal and righteous conduct — such is this harsh Time, plainly to be seen. The Bhagavat itself openly declares Time to be this terrible; even the mightiest are caught up and perish in its grip, such is the deceitfulness of maya. Therefore Trikamdas says: follow the guru's teaching; those without a guru have been defeated in this world.

On how Time entrapped the Sanakadik, Jivanji Maharaj gives this sakhi:

_To baaher nirgun dekhiye, bhitar gun bhandaar |
Him taadhu Jivanaa, pan jaale sab sansaar ||_
(Outwardly it may appear to carry no harmful quality, yet within it holds a whole store of destructive power. Frost, O Jivan, is cold, yet it burns the entire world.)

Jivanji Maharaj says that, seen from the outside, a thing may not appear to carry any harmful fault, yet when the frost falls, it possesses a quality that scorches the whole world.

In elaborating this sakhi, the Samagam writes that through three yugas the dharma of the Sanakadik held great glory — in Satyug the glory of truth, in Tretayug of austerity, in Dwaparyug of worship and ritual reverence — but when this terrible Kaliyug comes, the elixir of devotion to Vishnu will arise;

then, should they wander about as Vaishnavs, they will not attain the soul's liberation swiftly; if they take up the notion of "I am Brahman," the soul's liberation, too, will not come swiftly. For this reason, having drawn them out in this way, Bhagwan arranged to bring false blame and disgrace upon the Sanakadik, to bring them low, and so he set up the occasion by which the doorkeepers were made to pronounce the curse. So when the curse came about, Naradji and Lakshmiji began entreating Bhagwan to show grace; then Bhagwan set before Jay and Vijay two choices — if they wished for liberation after seven incarnations, they could attain it by practicing devotion to Vishnu with love; and if they wished for liberation after three incarnations, they could attain it by worshipping him instead through enmity. The Sanakadik understood that taking seven incarnations would mean a very long delay, whereas three incarnations would bring liberation sooner, and so they chose to worship through enmity. The reason they chose this hostile form of devotion was that the shadow of the Sanakadik, who had grown angry, was falling upon Jay and Vijay, and their understanding had been corrupted because of it.

In the Shiva Purana, chapter 58, shlok 11, it is stated which of the two — seven incarnations or three — the Sanakadik chose to take:

_Bhaktibhaavam samaasaadya saptaabhirjanmabhiriha |
Vairbhaave tathaa tribhiridam sthaanamavaapsyatha ||_
(Sanatkumar said: if you worship me with loving devotion, you will attain this abode after seven births; and if you worship me instead through enmity, you will attain this same abode again after three births.)

With reference to the curse of the sages, one sakhi says:

_Kapil munike kodhke, maare Sagar ke poot |
Sanakaadikne kodh kari, raakshas kiye Hari doot ||_
(Through Kapil Muni's anger, Sagar's sons were destroyed; and through the Sanakadik's anger, Hari's own doorkeepers were turned into rakshasas.)

Kapil Muni, through anger, burned to ashes the sixty thousand sons of Sagar; and, because of the anger of the sage Sanakadik, Bhagwan's own doorkeepers were turned into demons.

That whatever the manner in which one worships God, still one's welfare is achieved — on this there is a shlok:

_Gopyah kaamaadbhayaatkanso dveshaachchaidvaadayo nrupaah |
Sambandhaadvrushnayo yooyam sakhyaadbhaktyaa vayam vibho ||_
(O Lord! The gopis worship you through desire, Kansa through fear, Shishupal and other kings through enmity, the Yadavs through kinship, and we, the cowherds, through the devotion of friendship.)

O Lord! The gopis worship you through the emotion of desire, Kansa through fear, Shishupal and the rest of the kings through enmity, the Yadavs through the bond of kinship, and we cowherds through the devotion of friendship — in all these ways we are engaged in devotion to you.

Tulsidas has said that in whatever manner one practices devotion to Ram, still it bears fruit:

_Tulsi apne Ramko, reeji bhajo hai beej |
Khet pare par jaamihai, ulto sulto beej ||_
(Tulsi says: worship your own Ram, whether with love or otherwise, like a seed. A seed left lying in a field will sprout whether it fell right side up or upside down.)

Tulsidas says: whether you worship Ram with love or with anger, it still bears fruit, just as a seed lying fallen in a field, whether fallen upside down or the right way up, still sprouts. In the same way, your devotion, too, will bear fruit.

Even though they were Bhagwan's own doorkeepers, Jay and Vijay chose devotion through enmity, because the shadow of the angered Sanakadik lay upon them; and so, in the Samagam, it is said that if the shadow of Krishna himself should fall upon one, even then the intellect grows corrupted — there is a real fear of this, and on this a sakhi is given:

_Kabir chandan darpe lasanse, matahi bigaare vaas |
Sagraa darpe nagraase, puhi jugse darpe daas ||_
(Kabir says: sandalwood fears garlic, lest it spoil its own fragrance; those who honor the guru fear the guru-less, and, likewise, devotees go about fearing the delusion of the world.)

Das Kabirji says that sandalwood fears the foul smell of garlic, lest it should spoil its own sweet fragrance; in the same way, people who honor the guru's teaching fear those without a guru, lest such people lead them astray from the guru's path — in just this way devotees go about, fearing the maya of the world.

There is a shlok relating to this sakhi:

_Amitagunopi padaartho doshenaikena ninditobhavati |
Nishilarasaayamahito gandhenograna lashoona roopa ||_
(Even a thing endowed with countless good qualities becomes disparaged on account of a single flaw, just as garlic, though possessed of every fine medicinal property, is disparaged for its harsh odor.)

A thing may possess boundless good qualities, and yet, because of a single flaw, becomes an object of contempt — just as garlic, though endowed with the finest medicinal virtues, is condemned on account of its sharp, foul smell; so too, on account of a single flaw, one becomes an object of contempt.

The bad qualities of a wicked person never leave him; on this it is said:

_Jaako jeso subhaav, jaay nahi jivso |
Neemb na meethi hoy, seenchi gud dheevso ||_
(Whatever nature a person is born with does not leave him even to the end of his life; the neem tree does not turn sweet even if watered with jaggery and ghee.)

Whatever nature a person is born with does not leave him until the very end of his life, just as, even if a neem tree is watered with jaggery and ghee, its bitter fruit never turns sweet.

_Koila koi na ujlaa, navman saabun laai |
Moorakh ko samajhaavno, gyaan gaankko jaai ||_
(No amount of coal ever turns white, even if scrubbed with nine maunds of soap; trying to make a fool understand is like tying up one's own wisdom and throwing it away.)

Even if coal is washed with nine maunds of soap, it never turns white; in the same way, if one tries to make a fool understand something, the effort of counsel goes entirely to waste.

For this reason the virtuous wish to keep their distance, in fear, from the wicked; on this there is a sakhi:

_Dar vaaras dar param guru, dar karnime saar |
Khoji darai su ubre, gaafil paave saar ||_
(Fear is the truest inheritance, fear is the supreme teacher, fear is the essence of right conduct. He who lives in fear and searches carefully is saved; he who grows careless meets his ruin.)

Khojiji says that fear grants the capacity to keep clear of both virtue and vice going wrong; fear is the finest of teachers; there is safety only in walking with fear, for those who walk in fear are saved, while those who fall into carelessness suffer loss.

On what wretched fate befalls one who lives carelessly, the Samagam gives this sakhi:

_Kuvalayo maaro Jivanaa, kanse dino roy |
Taat bichaaro kaaka kare, janani haaltaavat mukh joy ||134||_
(When Krishna killed the elephant Kuvalayapida, O Jivan, it made Kansa weep. Poor Ugrasen, the father, could only mourn, and the helpless mother could only watch, her face full of grief.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that when Krishna killed the elephant Kuvalayapida, Kansa grew terrified, fearing that Krishna would now kill him too. That so sinful a son as Kansa was born was in no way the fault of his father Ugrasen, for it was Kansa's mother who, through adultery with Kaalpavan, became pregnant while yet Ugrasen's wife, and it was because of this that Kansa turned out so depraved — how, then, could poor Ugrasen, as a father, have made Kansa a person of good character?

There is a saying:

Sin does not stay hidden behind any curtain — in the end, it shows itself.
What can the poor father do, when the son's sin sends him to hell?
The father may bear with his son, but the sin itself does not spare him.

Kansa's mother committed her sin of adultery in secret, but in the end it showed itself in the bad qualities that appeared in her son Kansa, and poor Ugrasen, his father, could do nothing to defend him — his own son had to go to hell.

A father may put up with his own child's faults, but the sin itself does not fail to strike him.

There is a saying: one should never blame the enemy's side for bad news, nor should the messenger's ears be cut off for what he brings.

When bad news comes from the enemy's side, how can the one who merely brought the news be called at fault, and how can the poor messenger who delivered the bad tidings be punished for it?

Vyas composed a pad, in the raag Dhanashri, on how the son of an adulterous or irreligious person may himself be without devotion:

_Bhakt na bhayo bhaktko poot
Bhakt hoi saahat ke, jyo Shrutidev Sudama soot ||
Ugrasen ke hans, Bali ke Baanasur jam ut |
Bhisham ke sakam, Vibheeshan ke dhar bhayo kapoot ||
Sen, Dhanaa, Raidaas bhayo Jaydev, Kabir abhoot |
Boodyo bans Kabirkau, jab bhayo Kamalaa poot ||
Hoi bhakt ke saakat, jaaniyau anya kaahu kau moot |
Brahmaa ke Naarad, Vyaas ke Vidur Suk avdhoot ||284||_
(A devotee's own son does not always become a devotee: Ugrasen was a devotee, yet his son was Kansa; Bali was a devotee, yet his line brought forth Banasur, a foe of the god of death. [One phrase here, concerning Bhishma, is too worn in the source to render with confidence.] Vibhishan, too, was a devotee, yet his own son turned out wicked. On the other hand, a devotee may arise from anywhere, as with Shrutidev and Sudama's son: Sena, Dhana, and Raidas became devotees like Jaidev and the wondrous Kabir — yet even Kabir's own household name was tarnished when his son Kamal was born and proved otherwise. That a devotee's child should turn irreligious is no more remarkable than any ordinary thing. By contrast, Brahma's son was Narad, and among Vyas's own circle were Vidur and the sage Shuk, both great renunciates.)

[Bhakt Kavi Vyas, page 232]

In the Shiva Purana there is a shlok concerning the seven incarnations and the three incarnations.

Bhagwan told Jay and Vijay that if they worshipped him with unbroken devotion, their liberation would come after seven incarnations, and if they held enmity toward him, their liberation would come after three incarnations. They asked for devotion through enmity and chose the three incarnations. In these:

In the first incarnation, Jay became Hiranyaksha and Vijay became Hiranyakashyap.
In the second incarnation, they became Ravana and Kumbhakarna.
In the third incarnation, they became Dantavakra and Shishupal.

Since Lakshmiji wished to see the leela, she came as the Earth; when Hiranyaksha carried her off, the Sanakadik came in the form of Prahlad, and Bhagwan came in the forms of Varaha and Narsingh. In the second incarnation, when they came as Ravana and Kumbhakarna, the Sanakadik came as Vibhishan, Lakshmiji came in the form of Sita, and Bhagwan came in the form of Ram. In the third incarnation, when they came as Dantavakra and Shishupal, Lakshmiji came in the form of Rukmini; when Shishupal set about abducting Rukmini, Bhagwan came in the form of Krishna, and the Sanakadik came in the form of Bhishma. In this way Bhagwan showed his grace toward Lakshmi, and the fault of the Sanakadik...
